title: Probability-weighted ranking of 114 UK firms as buyers of a £60,000/year managed AI digital-employee service

weights.note: regulatory_risk is scored so 10 = LOW friction (a good thing). Weighted score is on a 1-10 scale.

method_notes: Affordability tests are anchored to ONS ASHE 2025 (April 2025, provisional) occupation medians: https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/bulletins/annualsurveyofhoursandearnings/2025

Employer on-cost loading of 1.25x (15% employer NIC above a £5,000 secondary threshold, 3% auto-enrolment pension, apprenticeship levy) is an ASSUMPTION. NIC change source: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/changes-to-the-class-1-national-insurance-contributions-secondary-threshold-the-secondary-class-1-national-insurance-contributions-rate-and-the-empl/changes-to-the-class-1-national-insurance-contributions-secondary-threshold-the-secondary-class-1-national-insurance-contributions-rate-and-the-empl

The 'signable without board approval' test used here is: the fee is at or below ~1% of firm revenue AND displaces at least ~1.5 admin FTE. The 1% delegation threshold is an ASSUMPTION (private-company delegation limits are not published); it is stated so the reader can replace it.

pilot_probability_12m is an ESTIMATE, not a measurement: p = 0.02 + (firm_score - 3) x 0.02, capped at 0.30. It describes the chance of one paid pilot within 12 months given a targeted approach to that named firm, and assumes warm introduction where available.

Firm scores = sector weighted score + scale adjustment (large +0.4, mid +0.1, small -1.0) + a named firm-specific adjustment where evidence exists. Scale for 30 property/field-service firms is classed from published footprint, not headcount - flagged in firm evidence.

Duncan & Toplis: 428 employees and £29.9m turnover in filed accounts = ~£69,900 revenue per head, so £60k is 0.2% of firm revenue at that size

claim_under_review.claim: Nick Vallescue (Dewey) is reported to have said UK and US healthcare are harder industries to sell AI/automation into.
claim_under_review.what_the_search_found: Searches for 'Vallescue', 'Nick Vallescue' and 'Dewey + AI + healthcare' return no relevant person, firm, interview, podcast transcript or article. The Dewey-like entities that do surface are unrelated: deweygroup.co.uk (Nottingham recruitment and training) and askdewey.com (a US consumer health AI site). No published source connects the name to a statement about healthcare sales difficulty.
claim_under_review.what_to_do: Do not repeat the quote as fact in any client-facing document. Treat it as an unverified recollection and argue the point from primary evidence, which is set out below.
claim_under_review.note: The absence of evidence is not evidence the person never said it - it means it cannot be cited. The substantive question is answered independently.

documented_barriers.what_it_requires: NHS organisations buy digital and IT through framework agreements. NHS England's own innovation guidance states: 'New suppliers cannot be added to an agreed procurement framework, except the Dynamic Purchasing System (DPS)'. Frameworks typically run up to four years and must be re-tendered.
documented_barriers.deal_impact: A small vendor cannot be bought by an NHS trust simply by persuading a department. It must already be on a framework, be added to a DPS, or wait for a further competition. This is a structural gate, not a sales objection.

documented_barriers.barrier: An incumbent framework already covers this exact service
documented_barriers.what_it_requires: NHS Shared Business Services runs the Intelligent Automation Framework Agreement (SBS10137), active 20 November 2023 to 19 November 2027, with Lot 1 intelligent automation services, Lot 2 software and licensing, and Lot 3 'intelligent automation as a service (IAaaS)'.
documented_barriers.deal_impact: The category is already procured, with suppliers already on the rail. A new entrant competes with IAaaS incumbents and cannot join the framework before it is re-let (November 2027).

documented_barriers.what_it_requires: DTAC is the NHS-recommended baseline assessment of safety, security, interoperability and usability for digital health technologies, and pulls in the NHS clinical risk management standards (DCB0129 for manufacturers, DCB0160 for deploying organisations).
documented_barriers.deal_impact: A compliance evidence pack must exist before the sale, not after. For a back-office agent this is proportionate only if the tool never touches clinical decision-making - and even then the buyer's IG team will ask for it.

documented_barriers.what_it_requires: An annual self-assessment against the National Data Guardian's standards for any organisation that accesses NHS patient data or systems. NHS buyers are required to check a supplier's DSPT status before awarding a contract, and to record it.
documented_barriers.deal_impact: The buyer's procurement file needs the supplier's DSPT position. Note the toolkit's own organisation types include 'Dentist' covering 'NHS clinical and educational dental services or private dental services', and 'Social Care' covering care homes - so DSPT exposure follows the organisation type, not only the contract.

documented_barriers.what_it_requires: Article 35 requires a DPIA where processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, including large-scale processing of special category data such as health data.
documented_barriers.deal_impact: Adds a 2-8 week step to every deployment and puts the DPO, not the operations director, in the approval path.

documented_barriers.what_it_requires: CQC does not assess or approve specific technologies, but holds registered providers accountable for safe, equitable, person-centred care. Its published AI position (updated 21 May 2026) lists hallucination, unclear accountability, de-skilling and human oversight as risks providers must manage.
documented_barriers.deal_impact: The provider's quality lead must be able to defend the tool to an inspector. That converts a line-of-business purchase into a governance project.

health_analysis.why_it_is_hard_in_one_paragraph: The demand is real - the NHS runs a dedicated intelligent automation framework precisely because back-office automation is wanted. The problem is that the fixed cost of becoming buyable (framework or DPS entry, DTAC evidence, a DCB0129 clinical safety case, DSPT, DPIA, CQC governance narrative) is largely independent of contract value. At £60,000 a year the vendor must amortise that cost over a single deal, while an incumbent on SBS10137 amortises it over an existing framework position. That is a unit-economics problem, not a demand problem.

is_uk_healthcare_a_poor_first_market.answer: Yes for NHS-facing healthcare; no for private-pay healthcare.
is_uk_healthcare_a_poor_first_market.for_nhs_facing: Poor first market. The gate is procurement (framework/DPS), the assurance stack is DTAC + DCB0129/0160 + DSPT + DPIA + CQC, and the framework that already covers the service is not re-let until 19 November 2027. A £60k ACV cannot carry that fixed cost, and a 9-18 month cycle is longer than a small vendor's runway. ASSUMPTION: the DTAC/clinical-safety evidence pack is 4-12 weeks of specialist work; it is not priced here.
is_uk_healthcare_a_poor_first_market.for_private_pay: Reasonable market, but only at group scale (30+ dental sites, 20+ care homes, multi-clinic aesthetics or occupational health). The NHS gate disappears; UK GDPR, DPIA and CQC do not.
conditions_where_nhs_is_worth_it: You are already on SBS10137 or another NHS framework
The buyer is an ICB or trust with a named budget line and an internal IG team that will sponsor the DTAC pack
You sell a clinical-adjacent tool with a medical-device classification and a regulatory pathway already mapped
You can treat the first NHS deal as a 12-month reference investment, not as revenue

health_analysis.conclusion: The caution is directionally right about NHS-facing healthcare and wrong as a blanket statement about healthcare. The barrier is the NHS procurement and assurance stack, not the sector's willingness to buy. Private-pay, non-NHS providers - above all veterinary and private dental groups - carry the same commercial logic as any other back-office buyer with far less gate.

substitute_sectors.why: Passes all four tests. (a) Affordability: six groups own >60% of UK practices and group EBITDA supports a £60k desk; (b) systems: the PMS estate is archaic (RoboVet partner-only integrations, on-prem Voyager, EXACT) and front-of-house staff handle up to 66% of client interaction; (c) dated trigger: the CMA's Veterinary Services Market Investigation Order 2026 imposed a statutory deadline for remedial action of 23 September 2026, with price lists, written estimates over £500 and itemised bills now mandatory, and out-of-hours providers reporting compliance from 15 October 2026; (d) no NHS gate and no special-category patient data - animal records are not health data under UK GDPR.

drop_list.sector: Healthcare administration (NHS-facing: private hospitals with NHS contracts, NHS GP groups, NHS dental)
drop_list.reason: The NHS procurement and assurance stack is a fixed cost larger than a £60k contract can amortise: framework/DPS gate, DTAC with DCB0129/0160 clinical safety, DSPT, DPIA, CQC governance, and an IA framework already covering the service until 19 November 2027.
drop_list.what_would_change_it: A route onto SBS10137 or a DPS, a buyer with a named budget and an internal IG sponsor, or a product that is explicitly non-clinical and hosted entirely outside NHS systems.
